Pictograph of two hands opening the bolt on a door.
張也。从門从幵。

Ideogrammic compound (會意 /会意): 門 (“door”) + 一 (“latch and/or wooden pole that shuts a door”) + 廾 (“a pair of hands”) — a pair of hands opening a latched door. 一 and 廾 are combined into 开 since the Small Seal script; however, in the conservative variant 𨵑, the two hands and the latch are well visible.
Compare 闢. See also 關, in which the door is kept shut by two wooden poles.
According to STEDT, from Proto-Sino-Tibetan *m/s-k(w)a-j (“mouth; opening; spread; door; face; jaw”). Cognate with 戶 (OC *ɡʷaːʔ, “door”), Tibetan ཁ (kha, “mouth”), Tibetan སྒོ (sgo, “door”).
The word is possibly a colloquial variant of 闓 (OC *ŋ̊ʰɯːlʔ, *ŋ̊ʰɯːls) (Schuessler, 2007). Proto-Mienic *kʰu̯ɔiᴬ (“to open”) (whence Iu Mien kʰɔi¹) and Thai ไข (kǎi) are Chinese loans (Ratliff, 2010).
Borrowed from English K (“karat”).

evidence.source: Shuowen.org, Shuowen Jiezi and Duan Yucai's commentary
evidence.field: 開 entry; seal-script reading and formation; Duan note
evidence.text: The received Shuowen entry gives 開 as 張也 (“to stretch/open”) and analyzes it as 从門从幵. Duan Yucai's commentary instead analyzes 幵 as the sound element, notes that the received fanqie 苦哀切 reflects a later reading, and offers a different historical phonological account. The same entry records 𨴉 as an old form and explains its 一 as a closed door and its lower element as a hand opening it. This documents competing analyses; it does not independently prove the popular two-hands-and-latch interpretation of 開.
evidence.title: 說文解字「開」 - Shuowen.org

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Taiwan, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: A04376 開, 說文釋形, 字樣說明, meanings
evidence.text: The entry reproduces both the Great Xu text analysis 从門从幵 and Duan's 从門、幵聲. It says the regular-script form is written from 幵, though the standard glyph uses a customary form inside 門. Its senses include opening/unlatching, spreading, expansion, founding, instruction, beginning, release, separation and others; cited literary examples span classical and later texts. The listed witnesses are dictionary quotations, not a complete dating of the semantic history.
evidence.title: [A04376] 開 - Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

evidence.source: Fudan University Center for the Study of Excavated Texts and Paleography, Wang Ning
evidence.field: Discussion of 開 and excavated manuscript forms, especially paragraphs 97-127
evidence.text: Wang argues that 幵 may itself be an early form used for the word 開, and cites occurrences interpreted as 開 in Warring States manuscripts, the Qin Shuihudi 日書 slips, and a Western Zhou bronze inscription. The article disputes proposals that the 門 component plus 幵 form arose through scribal corruption: it points to Warring States manuscript forms with 門 and 幵. It further proposes that early uses of 開 could favor senses such as instruct, explain or release, with 啟 more common for opening doors, while acknowledging growing overlap later. This is a scholarly argument, not uncontested proof of the graph's origin or a complete first-attestation record.
evidence.title: 王寧：清華簡八《攝命》中的所謂“啟”字別議——兼說“開”的相關問題

evidence.source: 漢典 (zdic.net), 開 entry and cited Shuowen/Kangxi material
evidence.field: 開 explanatory senses, Shuowen quote, received character variants
evidence.text: The entry gives 開 as 張也 in Shuowen and lists later senses including opening, blossoming, establishing, expanding, instructing, beginning and separating, with quotations attributed to pre-Qin, Han, Tang, Song and later texts. Its graph evolution panel labels Shuowen, Qin slips and regular script, but does not establish a secure earliest attestation date for the word or graph. The page's popular description of two doors, a latch and hands is an interpretation of small-seal form, not direct evidence for the graph's earliest formation.
evidence.title: 開 - 漢典

evidence.text: Local rows give 開 kāi, Middle Chinese khoj, Old Chinese *Nə-[k]ʰˤəj (intransitive) and *[k]ʰˤəj (transitive); 幵 has no row in this dataset. A separate local 幵 entry in the dataset is absent, so no same-system Old Chinese comparison between 開 and 幵 can be reported from this source. The dataset's notation is preserved as found.
evidence.title: Local Baxter–Sagart table cross-checked against Shuowen.org entry

evidence.source: 国务院, 汉字简化方案, via Wikisource transcription
evidence.text: The 1956 scheme's first list explicitly pairs 开（開）. This supports treating 开 as the standardized simplified counterpart of 開, rather than inferring that relation solely from similar appearance. The document dates the formal scheme to 1956; it does not date the earlier informal history of simplified variants.
evidence.title: 汉字简化方案

evidence.text: This secondary character page describes 開 as an associative compound of 廾, 門 and 一, with hands opening a door latch; it calls 开 a unique simplification by omission of part of 開. The familiar hands-and-latch reading is therefore attested as a modern explanatory account, but conflicts with Duan's phonetic analysis of 幵 and should not be presented as settled paleographic fact.
evidence.title: 開 Character Etymology - YellowBridge

evidence.text: Unicode states that its Unihan lookup provides individual ideograph properties including readings and that the database may be queried by code point. Direct character-specific GetUnihanData requests for U+5F00 and U+5E75 failed through the web tool; the accessible general lookup page cannot substantiate either character's kMandarin value. The local complete Unihan readings file was absent, and the tracked HSK extract did not contain either character. Thus current official Unihan readings could not be verified here.

evidence.field: Discussion of 開, 幵, and excavated manuscript forms
evidence.text: Wang Ning argues that forms written from 門 and 幵 occur in Warring States material, citing Shangbo IX 《陳公治兵》 slip 16 and Qin Shuihudi 《日書》 slips 128 and 134; he rejects an account in which that structure arose only through scribal corruption. He also proposes early semantic uses such as instructing, explaining, or releasing, with 啟 more commonly used for opening doors. This is a scholarly argument based on cited examples, not a comprehensive first-attestation chronology or uncontested formation account.

editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

gaps: No independently verified oracle-bone attestation for 開 was found. Do not claim an oracle-bone origin or a first-attested date from the available material.

The popular hands-and-latch explanation is not settled: Shuowen's received wording is ambiguous between semantic 幵 and phonetic 幵; Duan Yucai supports the phonetic interpretation. Early graphic evidence sufficient to resolve the formation remains unavailable here.

Wang Ning's paper advances a distinct account, including 幵 as an earlier graph for the 開 word and early semantic specialization, but these remain arguments requiring evaluation against the cited excavated artifacts and broader paleographic literature.

No exact dated first occurrence for the opening sense is established. Dictionary examples and Wang Ning's discussion point to pre-Qin and excavated manuscript usage, but do not provide a comprehensive earliest-attestation chronology.
Local Baxter–Sagart table contains 開 readings but no 幵 entry, so same-system historical phonetic comparison is unavailable. Do not infer a sound relationship from Mandarin readings.

The complete local Unihan readings file was absent and HSK extract lacked 开 and 幵. Unicode individual record pages were attempted but inaccessible via the browsing tool; current kMandarin readings for either character remain unverified. No character-specific Unicode records could be cited as verified evidence.
CUHK Multi-function Chinese Character Database result could not be opened; its search-result snippet raised a related 啟 analysis but was excluded from substantive claims.
No bulk data reuse terms were investigated because no repeated-source extract was recommended; character-specific pages and concise paraphrases suffice for this pass.

No usable, character-specific historical glyph image URL with verified identity and provenance was retrieved. The Xiaoxuetang query page opened but its form labels and image links were not exposed by the web tool; its general CC0 notice alone is insufficient to select an image. The Commons search yielded an unrelated 舍 file, so no glyph candidates are proposed.

No independently verified oracle-bone attestation or secure first-attested date for 開 was established in this pass. Wang Ning cites Warring States and Qin manuscript examples and a Western Zhou bronze case, but the earliest word sense and graph date remain unresolved.

The popular hands-and-latch interpretation conflicts with the phonetic analysis of 幵 attributed to Duan Yucai. The small-seal and received dictionary evidence do not settle the original formation or rule out all corruption proposals.

No exact dated semantic chronology was established. Wang Ning's proposed early uses and the cited manuscripts do not prove that the opening sense arose later; a dictionary's list of glosses cannot establish chronology.
The attempted Unicode individual records for U+5F00 and U+5E75 could not be opened; current official kMandarin values remain unverified in this pass.
